verdict.summary: Composio has no managed X app, so you have to register your own in the X Developer Console. No marketplace listing or security review is documented for standard OAuth 2.0 apps. What gets in the way is cost (pay-per-use credits, phone verification) and policy: self-serve plans are meant for apps with a limited number of end users, while scaled, government or AI-reply use cases need Enterprise access or X's written approval.
verdict.time_to_first_connection: About 30 min if your developer account is approved right away (one older X page says access is immediate; the changelog says approval is required)
verdict.approval_wait: None documented for OAuth installs. Developer-account approval may apply and is unconfirmed. Third-party reports put manual reviews at hours to days. Public Utility and Enterprise access go through manual, case-by-case review with no published timeline.

gates.name: Approved developer account + your own app
gates.unlocks: You can create an OAuth 2.0 app, connect your own X account through Composio, and make API calls that are billed against your credits.
limits: X's changelog says you need an approved developer account to create apps
Credentials are shown only once; regenerating them invalidates the old ones
Pay-per-use: you must buy credits before calls succeed (for example $0.005 per post read, $0.015 per post created, $0.200 per post created with a URL)
More than 10 apps requires an elevation request; a third-party blog reports a cap of 3 app creations per day (unverified)
gates.time_to_reach: 30-60 min, plus any developer-account approval wait (unconfirmed)

gates.name: Other X users authorize your app (no test-user allowlist documented)
gates.unlocks: Any X user you send through the authorize flow can grant the scopes you request. The findings show no test-user list or unlisted mode.
limits: Access tokens last 2 hours unless you request offline.access, which also issues a refresh token
The consent screen lists every scope you request
Rate limits apply per user for user-token calls and per app for app-only calls; most windows reset every 15 minutes, and going over returns HTTP 429
Pay-per-use is capped at 3 million post reads per monthly billing cycle

gates.name: Production use under self-serve pay-per-use, or Enterprise / Public Utility
gates.unlocks: Any X user can connect. No marketplace or app-store review is documented for standard OAuth apps. Scaled usage, government end users, or free scaled access each go through a separate application.
limits: Self-serve plans are meant for prototypes and apps with a limited number of end users; going beyond that requires applying for Enterprise
X can review your usage at any time and require a tier change
Showing or delivering X content to government-related entities requires Enterprise
Free scaled access (Public Utility apps) is decided by manual, case-by-case review
A third-party guide says AI-generated automated replies need X's prior written approval
X can suspend access without notice for violations
gates.time_to_reach: Same day on pay-per-use. Enterprise and Public Utility: manual review with no published timeline.

steps.title: Sign in to the X Developer Console and accept the Developer Agreement
steps.detail: Go to console.x.com, sign in with the X account that will own the app, and accept the Developer Agreement. If you accept on behalf of a company, you must have authority to bind it. The changelog says developer accounts need approval; if yours is not usable straight away, wait for approval.
gotchas: developer.x.com sends signed-out visitors to an X login page
It is unclear whether a new 2026 signup is approved instantly or needs review

steps.title: Verify a phone number and buy pay-per-use credits
steps.detail: Paid Services require a verified phone number. Buy credits in the Developer Console; every request draws them down. There are no subscriptions, contracts or minimum spend.
gotchas: Creating a post that contains a URL costs $0.200, compared with $0.015 for a plain post
The legacy Free, Basic and Pro tiers are reported closed to new developers

steps.title: Draft the app description and use case
steps.detail: Have an agent write the app name, description and an honest use-case statement. Cover how you will use X data, which actions you take (posting, liking, following, DMs), whether X content is shown outside X, and whether any government entity receives it. Register one app per use case; separate dev, staging and prod apps for the same service are allowed.
gotchas: Registering multiple apps for the same or overlapping use cases is prohibited
Government end users require Enterprise and must be named when you submit the use case

steps.title: Create the app in the Developer Console
steps.detail: Create a new app and enter the name, description and use case. Generate the credentials.
gotchas: Credentials are shown only once, so save them immediately

steps.title: Enable OAuth 2.0 and pick the Web App type
steps.detail: Open the app's authentication settings and enable OAuth 2.0. Choose Web App (a confidential client), which issues both a Client ID and a Client Secret for Composio. Native App and Single Page App are public clients that use PKCE only and get no secret.
gotchas: X API v2 user-context endpoints require OAuth 2.0, not OAuth 1.0a

steps.title: Register the callback URL
steps.detail: In the app's authentication settings, add the callback URL from your Composio auth config. The default is https://backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add. It must match exactly, including any trailing slash.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: An unregistered callback fails with error 415 'Callback URL not approved for this client application'
Each app can have at most 10 callback URLs; production URLs must use https; for local testing use http://127.0.0.1, not localhost

steps.title: Store the Client ID and Client Secret securely
steps.detail: Copy the OAuth 2.0 Client ID and Client Secret into a secrets manager. Do not share them with third parties, and tell X immediately if you suspect a breach.
gotchas: If you lose the credentials, regenerating them invalidates the old ones and breaks existing configs

steps.title: Trim the scope list
steps.detail: Composio's default list is broad: it includes dm.*, follows.write, block.write and more. Cut it down to what your agent actually uses, and keep offline.access so Composio can refresh tokens after 2 hours. If you need email, add users.email yourself; it is not in Composio's defaults.
gotchas: Users see every scope you request on the consent screen
Changing permissions later means users must re-authorize

steps.title: Create a Composio auth config with your own credentials
steps.detail: In Composio, create an auth config for the twitter toolkit using OAuth2 with your own Client ID and Client Secret and your trimmed scopes. Composio has no managed X app, so this step is required.

steps.title: Test the connection with your own account
steps.detail: Start a connection through Composio, sign in with your X account, approve the scopes, and make a test call such as reading your own user. Check that a refresh token was issued.
gotchas: The authorization code expires after 30 seconds, so slow manual code exchange will fail
An invalid client_id still shows the X login page rather than an immediate OAuth error, so a client_id mistake only surfaces after you log in

steps.title: Invite other users and monitor rate limits and spend
steps.detail: Send other users through the same Composio connect flow. Watch for HTTP 429 responses (most windows are 15 minutes, per user or per app) and watch your credit usage against the 3 million post-read monthly cap.

steps.title: Check production compliance before a wide launch
steps.detail: Review the Developer Agreement, Restricted Use Rules, Automation Rules and Display Requirements. Get explicit user consent before sending automated replies or DMs, label bot accounts under Settings > Your account > Automation, and do not train foundation models on X content. If you expect more than a limited number of end users, serve government users, or post AI-generated replies, apply for Enterprise access or X's written approval.
gotchas: X can review your usage at any time, require a tier change, or suspend you without notice

steps.title: Optional: request free Public Utility access
steps.detail: Non-commercial public-good apps can ask for free scaled access. X decides manually, case by case, per app, and publishes no timeline.

scopes.effect: Basic read access. No extra review is documented.
Lets the app post. Each post is billed ($0.015, or $0.200 with a URL), and automated or AI replies fall under the Automation Rules and consent rules.
Issues a refresh token. Without it, access tokens expire after 2 hours.
Included in Composio's defaults. Users see it on the consent screen; automated DMs need explicit user consent. The findings don't say whether it triggers extra review.

Included in Composio's defaults. Drop them unless you need them, since every scope appears on the consent screen.

blockers.symptom: Error 415: 'Callback URL not approved for this client application'
blockers.cause: The redirect URI doesn't exactly match a registered callback URL.
blockers.fix: Add the exact Composio callback URL, including any trailing slash, in the app's authentication settings.

blockers.symptom: Token exchange fails with an invalid or expired code
blockers.cause: The authorization code expires after 30 seconds.
blockers.fix: Let Composio exchange the code automatically, and retry the flow without manual delays.

blockers.symptom: Connections stop working after about 2 hours
blockers.cause: offline.access wasn't requested, so no refresh token was issued.
blockers.fix: Add offline.access to the scopes and have users reconnect.

blockers.cause: Per-user or per-app rate limit exceeded; most windows are 15 minutes.
blockers.fix: Back off until the window resets, and spread calls across users where possible.

blockers.symptom: You can't create an app in the console
blockers.cause: The developer account isn't approved yet, or you've hit the 10-app limit.
blockers.fix: Wait for account approval, or submit an elevation request that explains each app's use case.

blockers.cause: A policy violation, or X believes there is legal exposure.
blockers.fix: Check your email for a notice from the X platform team and appeal through the X Platform Help Form.

composio.note: Composio offers no managed X app, so you have to register your own X OAuth 2.0 app (Web App type) and enter its Client ID and Secret in a Composio auth config. Register Composio's callback URL (default https://backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add). Trim the broad default scope list, and keep offline.access. X's Developer Agreement bars providing API use on a service-bureau or managed-services basis, so if you serve multiple customers, each customer may need its own X app (bring-your-own-app).

open_questions: Does a new developer account signup in 2026 get approved instantly or go through review? The changelog and an older support page disagree. Check at console.x.com.
The console screens and field names (console.x.com) were not verified directly.
Do sensitive scopes such as dm.read, dm.write or users.email trigger any extra review? Nothing was documented.
Refresh-token lifetime and rotation behavior are not documented in the pages found.
There is no explicit number for what counts as a 'limited number of end users' before X requires Enterprise.
Is there an install or user cap for new apps, or a test-user mode? None was found.
No timeline was found for Public Utility or Enterprise review. The Government End User Request Form route comes only from a community post.
The AI-reply written-approval requirement comes from a third-party source and was not confirmed on an official X page.
Is a bring-your-own-app model required for multi-tenant products (third-party report, f63)? This depends on how X reads the service-bureau clause for your product.
